summary.text: The title page and table of contents of WHO's June 2005 guideline for manufacturers on pre-qualification of single-use injection devices under the PQS (Performance, Quality, Safety) system.

sections.title: Glossary

summary.text: A glossary of acronyms used in the PQS guideline, such as AD syringe, GHTF, GMP and ISO, followed by the start of the introduction. The introduction explains that the guideline tells manufacturers how to apply to WHO for pre-qualification of single-use injection devices and how to keep or lose that status.

sections.title: Background

summary.text: Explains why WHO recommends single-use injection devices, including auto-disable syringes, for infection control, and recalls the joint UNFPA, UNICEF and WHO statement that only auto-disable syringes should be used for immunization from 2003. It describes the roles of UN agencies and the medical device industry in securing a reliable supply.

sections.extract: In order to achieve effective infection control for intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular needle injections, WHO recommends the use of single-use injection devices. Single-use injection devices include single-use syringes used in conjunction with single-use needles, auto-disable (AD) syringes originally designed specifically for immunization, and syringes with a reuse-prevention feature for general purpose. sections.title: What is the PQS system?

summary.text: Describes the PQS system's origins in the WHO/UNICEF Product Information Sheets, used since 1979 to specify and test immunization equipment. It explains that conforming products will be listed as pre-qualified in an online database and catalogue.

summary.text: Explains transitional arrangements: from 30 June 2005 UN agencies will in principle buy only devices pre-qualified under the new procedure, with auto-disable and reuse-prevention syringes required to meet the relevant ISO 7886 standards.

sections.title: Pre-qualification of syringes for general purpose use

summary.text: States that only auto-disable and reuse-prevention syringes will be pre-qualified at first, with therapeutic and insulin devices to be considered in July 2006.

sections.extract: Pre-qualification of syringes for general purpose use In the first stage of implementation of the PQS only AD syringes for fixed dose immunization and syringes with a reuse-prevention feature will be prequalified under the PQS system. sections.title: What does PQS pre-qualification mean?

summary.text: Explains what pre-qualification means: it shows a device is technically suitable for UN procurement but does not guarantee purchase. Purchasers may add their own specifications, which must not conflict with ISO standards.

sections.extract: What does PQS pre-qualification mean? As noted in paragraph 3.2, injection devices currently listed under the PIS system will, in principle, not longer be purchased by UN procurement agencies after 30 June 2005, unless they have been pre-qualified under the PQS system. 2 The 2000 edition of the Product information Sheets can be downloaded from the WHO website at: www.who.int/vaccines-documents/DocsPDF00/www518.pdf

sections.title: What products are eligible for pre-qualification?

summary.text: Defines which syringes are eligible for pre-qualification, requiring compliance with specific ISO standards for therapeutic, fixed-dose immunization and insulin syringes. It notes that needles are not yet covered as a separate category.

sections.extract: What products are eligible for pre-qualification? Devices that conform to one of the two categories described in this section are potentially eligible for pre-qualification. Compliance with one of the two listed ISO standards is mandatory. Devices that only conform to national or regional standards are not eligible even if they do comply with the licensing and/or quality system standards set out in section 3.6.

sections.title: What are the minimum licensing requirements?

summary.text: Sets out minimum licensing requirements: devices licensed in a founding member of the Global Harmonization Task Force meet the quality criteria, while others must show conformity with listed quality system standards. Evidence must come from an accredited certification body as certified copies.

sections.extract: What are the minimum licensing requirements? sections.title: How do I apply for pre-qualification?

summary.text: Explains how to apply for pre-qualification by sending an introductory letter to the PQS Secretariat describing devices, standards and licensing, with 20 samples per device and site. WHO then either invites a formal application or advises that a device is unsuitable.

sections.extract: How do I apply for pre-qualification? sections.title: How do I prepare a product dossier?

summary.text: Explains how to prepare a product dossier, requiring a separate dossier for each device type, syringe volume and manufacturing site. It lists the required contents and the address for submission.

sections.extract: How do I prepare a product dossier? You must submit a separate and complete product dossier for each type of device that you have offered and which we have accepted as being suitable for evaluation. One dossier is required for each volume of syringe (for example, if you submit 1 ml, 2 ml and 5 ml syringes we will require three dossiers). sections.title: How much will I pay?

summary.text: Sets out cost-recovery fees for 2005: US$ 1000 for dossier examination and US$ 700 for each annual re-evaluation, charged per device.

sections.extract: How much will I pay? We will charge you on a cost recovery basis for the initial evaluation of your dossier. If your device is pre-qualified you will also be required to pay an annual re-evaluation fee as described in 3.11.2. The current fee scale, which will remain fixed until 31 December 2005, is shown in Table 3. (WHO will review the fee scale at the end of 2005). Table 3 - Cost recovery fees to be paid to WHO

sections.title: The dossier evaluation process

summary.text: Describes the dossier evaluation process, including a one-month grace period for missing items, possible use of independent evaluators under confidentiality, and acceptance of ISO-compliant devices without further testing.

sections.extract: The dossier evaluation process We will review the contents of your dossier. If anything is missing we will contact you in writing giving you a period of one month to provide the missing information, dossier fee or samples. If you fail to respond by the end of this period of grace we will return your dossier; the dossier examination fee will not be refunded. In addition we will not evaluate your dossier until the

sections.title: Evaluation results and the approval process

summary.text: Describes how evaluation results are reviewed and decided by the PQS Steering Group within six weeks of a complete dossier, and how manufacturers are told of approval or rejection, with decisions final.

sections.extract: Evaluation results and the approval process The PQS Secretariat will monitor the evaluation process and will endeavour to process applications as rapidly as resources allow; it will receive and review the evaluation results. sections.title: Maintaining pre-qualified status

summary.text: States that pre-qualified products are kept under continual review and that manufacturers must report significant changes to product, process or site or risk losing their status.

sections.extract: Maintaining pre-qualified status The performance of your product and of your company will be kept under continual review through the formal PQS review procedure and throughout the procurement process at the various UN procurement agencies. It is essential that you keep us fully informed about any significant change you make to the specifications of the product, to the manufacturing process or to the manufacturing

sections.title: The extra-ordinary PQS review process

summary.text: Describes extraordinary reviews when serious problems such as adverse events or device failures arise, which may lead to suspension or withdrawal of pre-qualification.

sections.extract: If serious problems arise with the product, leading to vigilance reporting, we reserve the right to re-evaluate your pre-qualification status at any time. A serious problem is an adverse event, device failure or other circumstance requiring immediate action. Generally, we will tell you about the problem and ask you to resolve it by an agreed date. However, if the problem is severe, we may suspend your

sections.title: The annual PQS review process

summary.text: Describes the annual review of pre-qualified devices against a standard checklist, with manufacturers required to pay the re-evaluation fee and submit renewed documents on time. Results are communicated only if problems are found or status changes.

sections.extract: All PQS pre-qualified injection devices will be reviewed once a year at a single fixed time, that will be communicated to you at the time prequalification is granted, against a standard checklist based on Annex 4.3. The annual review process will consider all relevant aspects of your device, including those referred to in Section 3.12. If we have previously highlighted problems which you need to resolve by an agreed

sections.title: Loosing pre-qualified status

summary.text: Lists the ways a manufacturer can lose pre-qualified status, such as unapproved changes to site, process or specification, poor quality reports from UN agencies, failure to report adverse events or renew licences, and bankruptcy.

sections.extract: Loosing pre-qualified status There are several ways in which you could loose your status as a pre-qualified manufacturer. These include, but are not confined to, the following: • if you change the manufacturing site with or without notifying us of your intention to do so (Annex 5.2, clause 8); • if you change the manufacturing process in an unacceptable way (one that negatively effects the performance of the device)

sections.title: Checklists

summary.text: Introduces three checklists to help manufacturers submit the information needed at each stage of pre-qualification.

sections.extract: This section provides you with three checklists designed to ensure that you send us all the information that we require at each of the stages specified.

sections.title: Annex 5.1 - Definitions

summary.text: Annex 5.1 giving definitions used in the PQS guideline, such as adverse event, certification body, certified copy and device, with some definitions derived from EU directives and ISO standards.

sections.extract: The following definitions apply to this document: Adverse event An incident resulting in permanent impairment, hospitalization, congenital malformation, injury or death to patients or users of a single-use injection device. Certification Body A Certification Body is a government department or agency or a third party organization that provides services for conformity assessment following completion of an independent

sections.title: Annex 5.2 – Standard Terms and Conditions

summary.text: Annex 5.2 setting out the standard terms and conditions for pre-qualification of single-use injection devices, which all manufacturers must follow. Clauses cover dossier screening, non-refundable fees, ongoing reporting of changes and adverse events, and grounds for suspension or withdrawal. Definitions of packaging terms such as unit container close the annex.

sections.extract: The Terms and Conditions and Definitions set out below will apply to all manufacturers of PQS pre-qualified injection devices. You should familiarize yourself with this document and ensure that you comply fully with the on-going reporting requirements set out therein.
